hook: The West Village puts *art on the menu*
dek: A Jamaican-American pastry star and the chef behind Eleven Madison Park opened blocks apart. Only one pours alcohol.

slides.label: Two openings
slides.text: This October, two West Village restaurants opened blocks apart, each treating the *art on the walls* as much the point as the food. One has *30 seats*. The other is about *5,000 square feet*.

slides.label: Calabash
slides.text: At 183 Christopher St., *Calabash* is the first solo restaurant from *Camari Mick*, a Le Bernardin and Eleven Madison Park alum and a Food & Wine *Best New Chef* in 2024.

slides.label: The menu
slides.text: Dinner is one 6:30 p.m. seating, a *$175* five-course prix fixe. Hoppin' John becomes collard green dolmas. Suya becomes a steak au poivre on *yaji spice* with plantain fries.

slides.label: The room
slides.text: Gallerist Cierra Britton curated work by *Black and brown artists*. Dinner opens with about a *half hour of canapés* inspired by the paintings, before anyone sits down.

slides.label: No alcohol
slides.text: Calabash pours *no alcohol*: a nonalcoholic sparkling rosé, house-brewed ginger beer, a *sorrel fizz*. In Caribbean homes, sorrel and ginger beer are *the holiday table*.

slides.label: Humm
slides.text: At 435 Hudson St., *Daniel Humm* opened *Humm* on Oct. 10. Art by Louise Bourgeois and Rashid Johnson, a *Francesco Clemente* ceiling mural and a rolling martini cart.

slides.label: The other side
slides.text: Humm's roast chicken for two runs *$108*. The Infatuation's review was *mixed*: it liked the chicken and the charred eggplant, but found the food *not quite as impressive* as the art.

slides.label: The Den's take
slides.text: Mick trained at Eleven Madison Park. Now she and Humm opened in the *same neighborhood, same month*. The ladder works sometimes, and people *build their own house*.

cta_line: The toast was never *only about the alcohol*.

caption_instagram:
Two of October's most talked-about openings landed blocks apart in the West Village, and both put art on the menu.

Calabash, at 183 Christopher St., is the first solo restaurant from Jamaican-American pastry chef Camari Mick, who trained at Le Bernardin and Eleven Madison Park. Dinner is a single 6:30 p.m. seating, a $175 five-course prix fixe that runs Hoppin' John, suya and jollof through a diaspora lens, under art by Black and brown artists curated by Cierra Britton. It pours no alcohol: sparkling NA rosé, house ginger beer, a sorrel fizz. A short walk away at 435 Hudson St., Daniel Humm opened Humm on Oct. 10, with works by Louise Bourgeois and Rashid Johnson, a Francesco Clemente ceiling mural, a $108 roast chicken for two and a rolling martini cart.

The other side: The Infatuation's Humm review was mixed, finding the food not quite as impressive as the art.

caption_linkedin:
Two West Village openings show how New York dining is being sold in 2026: as a cultural event, not just a meal.

Camari Mick, a Food & Wine Best New Chef who trained at Eleven Madison Park, opened Calabash, a 30-seat Afro-Caribbean bakery and brasserie with a $175 single-seating dinner, curated art and no alcohol at all. Blocks away, Daniel Humm opened Humm, a roughly 5,000-square-foot room with museum-grade art and a rolling martini cart.

The business bet at Calabash stands out. Wine pairings usually carry a big share of the margin at that price point. Dropping alcohol entirely is a read on who is actually at the table, and a test of whether experience and story can carry the premium.

Can a premium dining experience hold its price without alcohol?
